source: Data were collected from a total of 31 participants between the ages of 18–34 (15 females, 16 males).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participant demographics in the study.

claim: The perception (movie-watching and story-listening) data from these participants have been previously reported (Baldassano et al., 2018).
source: The perception (movie-watching and story-listening) data from these participants have been previously reported (Baldassano et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement references a prior publication that reported on the same dataset.

claim: Due to data loss during the recall phase, one participant (female) was excluded from the recall analyses.
source: Due to data loss during the recall phase, one participant (female) was excluded from the recall analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusion criteria.

claim: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Princeton University.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Princeton University, and all participants provided their written informed consent (IRB #7225).

claim: All participants provided their written informed consent.
source: The experimental protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Princeton University, and all participants provided their written informed consent (IRB #7225).

claim: Each of the 16 stories described the schematic script of either eating at a restaurant or catching a flight at an airport.
source: Each of the 16 stories described the schematic script of either eating at a restaurant or catching a flight at an airport (Bower et al., 1979).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the stimulus design, with citation to prior work on these scripts.

claim: Restaurant stories followed a four-stage event structure consisting of entering and being taken to a table, sitting with menus, ordering food and waiting for its arrival, and food arriving and being eaten.
source: For restaurant stories, the event structure consisted of (1) entering and being taken to a table, (2) sitting with menus, (3) ordering food and waiting for its arrival, and (4) food arriving and being eaten
evidence: This is a direct description of the restaurant script structure used in the study.

claim: Airport narratives followed a four-stage event structure consisting of entering the airport, going through the security, walking to and waiting at the gate, and getting on board the plane and sitting in a seat.
source: while airport narratives consisted of (1) entering the airport, (2) going through the security, (3) walking to and waiting at the gate, and (4) getting on board the plane and sitting in a seat.
evidence: This is a direct description of the airport script structure used in the study.

claim: Each story, whether video or audio, was approximately 3 min long.
source: Each story, whether video or audio, was approximately 3 min long.
evidence: This is a direct statement about stimulus duration.

claim: Data were acquired with a voxel size of 2.0 mm isotropic and a TR of 1.5 s.
source: Data were acquired with a voxel size of 2.0 mm isotropic and a TR of 1.5 s (see Baldassano et al., 2018, for a full description of the sequence parameters).
evidence: This is a direct statement about fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Participants were informed that they would be asked to freely recall the stories after all 16 had been presented.
source: Participants were informed that they would be asked to freely recall the stories after all 16 had been presented.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental instructions given to participants.

claim: During the recall phase, participants were asked to freely verbally recall (at their own pace) the details of each story when cued by the title of the story-to-remember.
source: During the recall phase, participants were asked to freely verbally recall (at their own pace) the details of each story when cued by the title of the story-to-remember.
evidence: This is a direct description of the recall task procedure.

claim: There were four recall runs in total.
source: There were four recall runs in total.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: During each recall run, participants were cued to recall four stories, with a 1 min rest between each story recall.
source: During each recall run, participants were cued to recall four stories, with a 1 min rest between each story recall.
evidence: This is a direct description of the recall run structure.

claim: After recalling all 16 stories, while still being scanned, participants were asked to provide verbal descriptions of the typical experience of eating at a restaurant and the typical experience of going through an airport.
source: After recalling all 16 stories, while still being scanned, participants were asked to provide verbal descriptions of the typical experience of eating at a restaurant and the typical experience of going through an airport.
evidence: This is a direct statement about an additional task performed during scanning.

claim: Searchlights were generated by randomly sampling a center vertex of the fsaverage6 surface mesh and identifying all vertices within 11 steps from it.
source: Our searchlights were generated by randomly sampling a center vertex of the fsaverage6 surface mesh and identifying all vertices within 11 steps from it.
evidence: This is a direct description of the searchlight analysis method.

claim: The vertex spacing within the fsaverage6 mesh is 1.4 mm.
source: Because the vertex spacing within the fsaverage6 mesh is 1.4 mm, the resulting radius is 15 mm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the spatial resolution of the surface mesh.

claim: The resulting searchlight radius is 15 mm.
source: Because the vertex spacing within the fsaverage6 mesh is 1.4 mm, the resulting radius is 15 mm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the searchlight size, derived from the vertex spacing.

claim: This process yielded 1483 searchlights per hemisphere.
source: This process yielded 1483 searchlights per hemisphere.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of searchlights generated.

claim: The a priori ROIs included mPFC, PMC, SFG, AG, and PHC.
source: Following recent work on the encoding of narrative event schemas using the same encoding dataset (Baldassano et al., 2018), as well as prior research on the representation of high-level situation models (Zadbood et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Baldassano et al., 2017; Kurby and Zacks, 2008; Radvansky and Zacks, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2019; Clewett et al., 2019), we focused our main ROI analyses on mPFC, PMC, SFG, AG, and PHC because of their consistent presence in naturalistic paradigms and their role in maintaining schema representations during encoding.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ROIs selected, justified by prior literature.

claim: mPFC, PMC, SFG, AG, and PHC were selected as ROIs because of their consistent presence in naturalistic paradigms and their role in maintaining schema representations during encoding.
source: Following recent work on the encoding of narrative event schemas using the same encoding dataset (Baldassano et al., 2018), as well as prior research on the representation of high-level situation models (Zadbood et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Baldassano et al., 2017; Kurby and Zacks, 2008; Radvansky and Zacks, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2019; Clewett et al., 2019), we focused our main ROI analyses on mPFC, PMC, SFG, AG, and PHC because of their consistent presence in naturalistic paradigms and their role in maintaining schema representations during encoding.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for ROI selection, supported by citations.

claim: The full hippocampus ROI was extracted from a freesurfer subcortical parcellation.
source: Our full hippocampus ROI was extracted from a freesurfer subcortical parcellation, which was then further split between an anterior at y > –20 and posterior portion at y <= –20 in MNI space (Guo and Yang, 2020; Poppenk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method for defining the hippocampus ROI.

claim: The hippocampus was split between an anterior portion at y > –20 and posterior portion at y <= –20 in MNI space.
source: Our full hippocampus ROI was extracted from a freesurfer subcortical parcellation, which was then further split between an anterior at y > –20 and posterior portion at y <= –20 in MNI space (Guo and Yang, 2020; Poppenk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the hippocampus was subdivided, with citations to prior work using this approach.

claim: Encoding story scores were high across all of cortex.
source: Encoding story scores were high across all of cortex (Figure 2A; q < 0.05), including all of our cortical and hippocampal ROIs (all p<0.01), with the strongest effects in posterior sensory regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 2A and statistical testing.

claim: Encoding story scores were significant in all cortical and hippocampal ROIs (all p<0.01).
source: Encoding story scores were high across all of cortex (Figure 2A; q < 0.05), including all of our cortical and hippocampal ROIs (all p<0.01), with the strongest effects in posterior sensory regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical testing of ROI data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The strongest encoding story effects were in posterior sensory regions.
source: Encoding story scores were high across all of cortex (Figure 2A; q < 0.05), including all of our cortical and hippocampal ROIs (all p<0.01), with the strongest effects in posterior sensory regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by the spatial pattern of results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Strong encoding schema scores were obtained throughout the default mode network.
source: Strong encoding schema scores were obtained throughout the default mode network (Figure 2B; p<0.01 for all cortical ROIs).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 2B and statistical testing of ROIs.

claim: All cortical ROIs showed significant encoding schema scores (p<0.01).
source: Strong encoding schema scores were obtained throughout the default mode network (Figure 2B; p<0.01 for all cortical ROIs).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical testing of ROI data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There were strong schematic patterns in anterior but not posterior hippocampus at encoding.
source: Additionally, there were strong schematic patterns in anterior but not posterior hippocampus (p<0.01 for whole hippocampus and anterior hippocampus; p=0.28 for posterior hippocampus).
evidence: This statement is supported by statistical testing comparing anterior and posterior hippocampus.

source: Additionally, there were strong schematic patterns in anterior but not posterior hippocampus (p<0.01 for whole hippocampus and anterior hippocampus; p=0.28 for posterior hippocampus).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result.

claim: Encoding schema scores were significant in anterior hippocampus (p<0.01).
source: Additionally, there were strong schematic patterns in anterior but not posterior hippocampus (p<0.01 for whole hippocampus and anterior hippocampus; p=0.28 for posterior hippocampus).

claim: Encoding schema scores were not significant in posterior hippocampus (p=0.28).
source: Additionally, there were strong schematic patterns in anterior but not posterior hippocampus (p<0.01 for whole hippocampus and anterior hippocampus; p=0.28 for posterior hippocampus).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result.

claim: Significant reinstatement story scores were found in regions overlapping with the default mode network, particularly lateral posterior SFG, central middle temporal gyrus, PHC, and AG with strongest effects in PMC.
source: We found significant reinstatement story scores in regions overlapping with the default mode network (DMN), particularly lateral posterior SFG, central middle temporal gyrus, PHC, and AG with strongest effects in PMC (Figure 2C, q < 0.05).

evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

source: Our specific ROI analyses (Figure 2C) also showed strong reinstatement story scores in the same regions such as PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), AG (p=0.04) but not did not show effects in mPFC (p=0.42), SFG (p>0.5), nor any of our hippocampal ROIs (full: p>0.5; anterior: p>0.5; posterior: p=0.29).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

source: Our specific ROI analyses (Figure 2C) also showed strong reinstatement story scores in the same regions such as PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), AG (p=0.04) but not did not show effects in mPFC (p=0.42), SFG (p>0.5), nor any of our hippocampal ROIs (full: p>0.5; anterior: p>0.5; posterior: p=0.29).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

source: Our specific ROI analyses (Figure 2C) also showed strong reinstatement story scores in the same regions such as PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), AG (p=0.04) but not did not show effects in mPFC (p=0.42), SFG (p>0.5), nor any of our hippocampal ROIs (full: p>0.5; anterior: p>0.5; posterior: p=0.29).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

source: Our specific ROI analyses (Figure 2C) also showed strong reinstatement story scores in the same regions such as PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), AG (p=0.04) but not did not show effects in mPFC (p=0.42), SFG (p>0.5), nor any of our hippocampal ROIs (full: p>0.5; anterior: p>0.5; posterior: p=0.29).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

source: Our specific ROI analyses (Figure 2C) also showed strong reinstatement story scores in the same regions such as PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), AG (p=0.04) but not did not show effects in mPFC (p=0.42), SFG (p>0.5), nor any of our hippocampal ROIs (full: p>0.5; anterior: p>0.5; posterior: p=0.29).

claim: The searchlight analysis revealed positive reinstatement schema scores in left anterior temporal pole.
source: For schema reinstatement (Figure 2D), the searchlight analysis revealed positive reinstatement schema scores in left anterior temporal pole (AT) as well as a negative effect in areas overlapping with left lateral SFG, indicating that stories from the same schema were more differentiated in this region (vs. stories from different schemas).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The searchlight analysis revealed a negative reinstatement schema effect in areas overlapping with left lateral SFG, indicating that stories from the same schema were more differentiated in this region (vs. stories from different schemas).
source: For schema reinstatement (Figure 2D), the searchlight analysis revealed positive reinstatement schema scores in left anterior temporal pole (AT) as well as a negative effect in areas overlapping with left lateral SFG, indicating that stories from the same schema were more differentiated in this region (vs. stories from different schemas).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 2D and includes an interpretation of the negative effect.

claim: ROI analyses revealed strong schema reinstatement effects in anterior hippocampus (p<0.01).
source: Additionally, similar to our encoding results, our specific ROI analyses revealed strong schematic effects in anterior (p<0.01) but not posterior hippocampus (p>0.5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: ROI analyses did not reveal schema reinstatement effects in posterior hippocampus (p>0.5).
source: Additionally, similar to our encoding results, our specific ROI analyses revealed strong schematic effects in anterior (p<0.01) but not posterior hippocampus (p>0.5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Schema reinstatement effects were not found in mPFC (p>0.5).
source: In contrast to our encoding results, we did not find schema reinstatement effects in mPFC (Figure 2D, p>0.5) nor SFG (p>0.5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Schema reinstatement effects were not found in SFG (p>0.5).
source: In contrast to our encoding results, we did not find schema reinstatement effects in mPFC (Figure 2D, p>0.5) nor SFG (p>0.5).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Schema reinstatement effects were found in PMC (p<0.01).
source: However, we did find schema reinstatement effects in PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), and AG (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Schema reinstatement effects were found in PHC (p<0.01).
source: However, we did find schema reinstatement effects in PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), and AG (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Schema reinstatement effects were found in AG (p<0.01).
source: However, we did find schema reinstatement effects in PMC (p<0.01), PHC (p<0.01), and AG (p<0.01).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Encoding story scores predicted subsequent memory for story details in a very wide range of cortical regions.
source: Encoding story scores predicted subsequent memory for story details in a very wide range of cortical regions (Figure 3A, q < 0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Significant positive effects of encoding story scores on subsequent memory were found in all cortical and hippocampal ROIs (p<0.01 for all regions, except for p=0.03 for anterior hippocampus).
source: In agreement with the searchlight analysis, we also found significant positive effects in our cortical and hippocampal ROIs (Figure 3A, p<0.01 for all regions, except for p=0.03 for anterior hippocampus).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from ROI analysis.

claim: The correlation between encoding story scores and subsequent memory was significantly more positive for posterior vs. anterior hippocampus (t(58) = –74.74, p<0.001).
source: The correlation between encoding story scores and subsequent memory was significantly more positive for posterior vs. anterior hippocampus (t(58) = –74.74, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison between hippocampal subregions.

claim: The strongest positive effects of encoding schema scores on memory were found in regions overlapping with the left primary visual cortex, prostriata, anterior mPFC, entorhinal cortex, left posterior temporal sulcus, and left subcentral and postcentral gyrus.
source: Based on our searchlight results, the strongest positive effects were found in regions overlapping with the left primary visual cortex, prostriata, anterior mPFC, entorhinal cortex, left posterior temporal sulcus, and left subcentral and postcentral gyrus (Figure 3B, q < 0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Reverse effects (with more schematic information at encoding predicting poorer story-specific memory performance) were found in multiple regions including bilateral SPL.
source: Interestingly, we also found reverse effects (with more schematic information at encoding predicting poorer story-specific memory performance) in multiple regions including bilateral SPL (Figure 3B, q < 0.05).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No strong effects of encoding schema scores on recall behavior were found in cortical ROIs, including the broad mPFC ROI.
source: When we looked for correlations between encoding schema scores and recall behavior in our cortical ROIs, we did not find any strong effects (Figure 3B), including our broad mPFC ROI, despite finding a correlation between encoding schema scores and recall behavior in its most anterior portion via the searchlight analysis.
evidence: This statement is supported by the ROI analysis results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Significant negative effects of encoding schema scores on subsequent memory were found in posterior hippocampus (p<0.01).
source: Lastly, when we analyzed subsections of the hippocampus, we found opposite correlations between encoding schema scores and subsequent memory, with significant negative effects in posterior hippocampus (p<0.01) and numerically positive but nonsignificant effects in anterior hippocampus (p=0.27).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: Numerically positive but nonsignificant effects of encoding schema scores on subsequent memory were found in anterior hippocampus (p=0.27).
source: Lastly, when we analyzed subsections of the hippocampus, we found opposite correlations between encoding schema scores and subsequent memory, with significant negative effects in posterior hippocampus (p<0.01) and numerically positive but nonsignificant effects in anterior hippocampus (p=0.27).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical result from ROI analysis.

claim: The effects of encoding schema scores on subsequent memory in anterior and posterior hippocampus were significantly different from each other (t(58) = 107, p<0.001).
source: The effects in these two subregions were significantly different from each other when we compared their model coefficients (anterior – posterior) across participants (t(58) = 107, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison between hippocampal subregions.

claim: Reinstatement story scores were related to recall of specific story details in many regions, with the strongest effects in areas overlapping with bilateral PMC, right mPFC, and right AT cortex.
source: Reinstatement story scores were related to recall of specific story details in many regions, with the strongest effects in areas overlapping with bilateral PMC, right mPFC, and right AT cortex (Figure 3C).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Significant effects of reinstatement story scores on memory were found in mPFC, SFG, and AG ROIs.
source: These effects were also confirmed in our larger cortical ROIs: There were significant effects in mPFC, SFG, and AG, and the strongest effects were in PMC and PHC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from ROI analysis.

claim: The strongest effects of reinstatement story scores on memory in cortical ROIs were in PMC and PHC.
source: These effects were also confirmed in our larger cortical ROIs: There were significant effects in mPFC, SFG, and AG, and the strongest effects were in PMC and PHC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from ROI analysis.

claim: Reinstatement story scores in posterior and not anterior hippocampus positively predicted subsequent memory.
source: In our hippocampus ROIs, we found that reinstatement story scores in posterior and not anterior hippocampus positively predicted subsequent memory (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from ROI analysis.

claim: The effect of reinstatement story scores on memory for posterior hippocampus was significantly larger than the effect for anterior hippocampus (t(58) = –27.45, p<0.001).
source: the effect for posterior hippocampus was significantly larger than the effect for anterior hippocampus (t(58) = –27.45, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a statistical comparison between hippocampal subregions.

claim: The strongest significant effects of reinstatement schema scores on memory were in regions overlapping with bilateral primary visual cortices, bilateral posterior temporal sulcus, parietal regions, PHC, partial sections of medial SFG, right SPL, and lateral PFC.
source: In the searchlight analysis with reinstatement schema scores as a predictor variable, the strongest significant effects were in regions overlapping with bilateral primary visual cortices, bilateral posterior temporal sulcus, parietal regions, PHC, partial sections of medial SFG, right SPL, and lateral PFC (Figure 3D).
evidence: This statement is supported by the searchlight analysis results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There were no significant effects of reinstatement schema scores on memory in the a priori cortical or hippocampal ROIs.
source: There were no significant effects in the a priori cortical or hippocampal ROIs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical results from ROI analysis.

claim: Schematic representations in bilateral visual cortex, AG, and fusiform cortex at encoding were the best predictors of PMC's reinstatement story effect.
source: We found that, across the brain, schematic representations in bilateral visual cortex, AG, and fusiform cortex were the best predictors of PMC's reinstatement story effect.
evidence: This statement is supported by the ROI-to-ROI correlation analysis described in the text.

claim: During encoding, the conjunction analysis identified regions in visual cortex, left posterior temporal sulcus, prostriata, entorhinal cortex, left subcentral gyrus, postcentral sulcus, right lateral SFG, and anterior mPFC where schema scores were robustly activated and supported memory performance.
source: During encoding (Figure 4A), this conjunction analysis identified regions in visual cortex, left posterior temporal sulcus, prostriata, entorhinal cortex, left subcentral gyrus, postcentral sulcus, right lateral SFG, and anterior mPFC.
evidence: This statement is supported by the conjunction analysis results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For retrieval, the conjunction analysis found effects in visual cortex, posterior superior temporal sulcus, left fusiform gyrus, right SPL, right AG, PHC, medial SFG, and MFG where schema scores were robustly activated and supported memory performance.
source: For retrieval (Figure 4A), we found effects in visual cortex, posterior superior temporal sulcus, left fusiform gyrus, right SPL, right AG, PHC, medial SFG, and MFG.
evidence: This statement is supported by the conjunction analysis results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: One set of regions had significantly stronger relationships between schema scores and subsequent memory at encoding than at recall (portions of left visual cortex, left posterior temporal sulcus, right prostriata, entorhinal cortex, left subcentral cortex, postcentral sulcus, frontal gyrus, and portions of anterior mPFC).
source: This analysis corroborated our conjunction analysis (Figure 4A), revealing one set of regions that had significantly stronger relationships to subsequent memory at encoding than at recall (portions of left visual cortex, left posterior temporal sulcus, right prostriata, entorhinal cortex, left subcentral cortex, postcentral sulcus, frontal gyrus, and portions of anterior mPFC)
evidence: This statement is supported by the model coefficient comparison analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Another set of regions had significantly stronger relationships between schema scores and subsequent memory at recall than encoding (visual cortex, SPL, clusters in posterior parietal regions, SFG, regions in frontal gyrus, and PHC).
source: and another set of regions that had significantly stronger relationships to subsequent memory at recall than encoding (visual cortex, SPL, clusters in posterior parietal regions, SFG, regions in frontal gyrus, and PHC).
evidence: This statement is supported by the model coefficient comparison analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A silhouette analysis revealed that k = 2 yielded the highest average silhouette coefficient (s = 0.39) for clustering within mPFC.
source: We then ran a silhouette analysis on these eight-feature representations to determine the optimal number of clusters to use within a bilateral mPFC ROI mask (restricting the number of clusters k to be less than the number of input features). The analysis revealed that k = 2 yielded the highest average silhouette coefficient (s = 0.39).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the silhouette analysis.

claim: With the k = 2 solution, the two mPFC clusters separated along the anterior-posterior axis in both hemispheres.
source: With this k = 2 solution, we found that the two clusters separated along the anterior-posterior axis in both hemispheres (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is supported by the clustering results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both mPFC clusters exhibited story and schema effects at encoding.
source: We found that both clusters exhibited story and schema effects at encoding, but the contributions of these effects to subsequent memory differed across clusters
evidence: This statement is supported by the post-hoc analysis of the mPFC clusters.

claim: The encoding schema effect predicted subsequent memory in the anterior mPFC cluster but not the posterior cluster.
source: The encoding schema effect predicted subsequent memory in the anterior cluster but not the posterior cluster
evidence: This statement is supported by the post-hoc analysis of the mPFC clusters.

claim: The relationship between the encoding story effect and subsequent memory was much larger in the posterior mPFC cluster than the anterior cluster.
source: by contrast, the relationship between the encoding story effect and subsequent memory was much larger in the posterior cluster than the anterior cluster.
evidence: This statement is supported by the post-hoc analysis of the mPFC clusters.

claim: PMC reinstatement story scores were a significant partial mediator between mPFC_c0 encoding schema scores and rubric-derived memory scores (indirect effect A * B = 0.029, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap CI [0.006, 0.056]).
source: Indeed, we found that PMC story information acted as a partial mediator between mPFC_c0 schema information at encoding and later memory (indirect effect A * B = 0.029, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap CI [0.006, 0.056]).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the results from the mediation analysis.

claim: An anterior mPFC region showed a significant correlation between activation of schema representations at encoding and subsequent behavioral recall performance.
source: In keeping with this prediction, an anterior mPFC region showed a significant correlation between activation of schema representations at encoding and subsequent behavioral recall performance
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract summarizing a key finding.

claim: The anterior mPFC region implicated in schema representation at encoding was not implicated in schema representation during retrieval.
source: however, this mPFC region was not implicated in schema representation during retrieval.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract summarizing a key finding.

claim: The analyses revealed largely distinct brain networks at encoding and retrieval in which schema activation was related to successful recall.
source: More generally, our analyses revealed largely distinct brain networks at encoding and retrieval in which schema activation was related to successful recall.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract summarizing a key finding.

claim: Schematic prior knowledge can scaffold the construction of event memories during perception.
source: Schematic prior knowledge can scaffold the construction of event memories during perception and also provide structured cues to guide memory search during retrieval.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract about the theoretical framework.

claim: Schematic prior knowledge can provide structured cues to guide memory search during retrieval.
source: Schematic prior knowledge can scaffold the construction of event memories during perception and also provide structured cues to guide memory search during retrieval.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract about the theoretical framework.

claim: The cognitive psychology literature has shown that we leverage event schemas to support memory for specific details from those events.
source: Over the past half-century, the cognitive psychology literature has shown that we leverage event schemas – our knowledge of how events generally unfold – to support memory for specific details from those events (for reviews of early work, see Graesser and Nakamura, 1982; Alba and Hasher, 1983; Brewer and Nakamura, 1984; for more recent cognitive neuroscience studies, see van Kesteren et al., 2012; Ghosh and Gilboa, 2014; Schlichting and Preston, 2015; Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Wang and Morris, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: At encoding, the restaurant script can provide a scaffold onto which we can attach specific event details.
source: At encoding, the restaurant script can provide a scaffold onto which we can attach specific event details (e.g., Bransford and Johnson, 1972; Alba and Hasher, 1983; Abbott et al., 1985; Tompary and Thompson-Schill, 2021; McClelland et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: At retrieval, the restaurant script provides a structured way of cueing memory, by stepping through the various stages of the script in sequence.
source: later, at retrieval, the restaurant script provides a structured way of cueing memory, by stepping through the various stages of the script in sequence (e.g., Schank and Abelson, 1975; Anderson and Pichert, 1978; Bower et al., 1979; Alba and Hasher, 1983; Mandler, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: mPFC has been frequently implicated in previous schema research.
source: Because mPFC has been frequently implicated in previous schema research (e.g., van Kesteren et al., 2013; van Kesteren et al., 2010a; van Kesteren et al., 2020; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Baldassano et al., 2018; Raykov et al., 2020; Raykov et al., 2021; Reagh et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: mPFC has been implicated in integrating new knowledge into existing schemas.
source: Because mPFC has been frequently implicated in previous schema research (e.g., van Kesteren et al., 2013; van Kesteren et al., 2010a; van Kesteren et al., 2020; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Baldassano et al., 2018; Raykov et al., 2020; Raykov et al., 2021; Reagh et al., 2021) – in particular, with regard to integrating new knowledge into existing schemas (Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Schlichting and Preston, 2015; Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Tse et al., 2007; Wang and Morris, 2010; van Kesteren et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Prior work implicates the hippocampus in schema representation.
source: Based on prior work implicating the hippocampus in schema representation (van Kesteren et al., 2013; van Kesteren et al., 2020; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Brod et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Raykov et al., 2020; Webb et al., 2016; van der Linden et al., 2017; Bonasia et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Hippocampus has a coarse-to-fine gradient of representations along its long axis.
source: based on work showing that hippocampus has a coarse-to-fine gradient of representations along its long axis (Collin et al., 2015; Guo and Yang, 2020; Audrain and McAndrews, 2020; Poppenk et al., 2013; Brunec et al., 2018; Schlichting et al., 2015; Sekeres et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Anterior hippocampus has coarser and thus more general representations than posterior hippocampus.
source: we predicted that anterior hippocampus (which has coarser and thus more general representations than posterior hippocampus) would contain schematic representations that contribute to subsequent memory
evidence: This statement is based on inference from prior literature about hippocampal gradients.

claim: Posterior hippocampus would contribute to subsequent memory by representing story-specific details.
source: whereas posterior hippocampus would contribute to subsequent memory by representing story-specific details.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior literature about hippocampal gradients.

claim: Posterior hippocampus showed a negative correlation between schema representation at encoding and subsequent memory.
source: While the degree of schema representation in anterior hippocampus during encoding showed a nonsignificant, positive numerical relationship to subsequent memory for story details, posterior hippocampus showed a negative correlation between schema representation at encoding and subsequent memory
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding.

claim: Posterior hippocampus showed a positive correlation between the representation of story-specific details at encoding and subsequent memory.
source: and a positive correlation between the representation of story-specific details at encoding and subsequent memory
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding.

claim: The set of regions where schema representation at encoding predicted recall of story details was mostly distinct from the set of regions where schema representation at retrieval predicted recall of story details.
source: Interestingly, the set of regions where schema representation at encoding predicted recall of story details was mostly distinct from the set of regions where schema representation at retrieval predicted recall of story details
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding.

claim: The network where schema representation at retrieval predicted recall included bilateral visual cortex, right superior parietal lobule (SPL), bilateral middle frontal gyrus (MFG), bilateral medial SFG, bilateral parahippocampal cortex (PHC), left fusiform gyrus, right angular gyrus (AG), as well as bilateral posterior superior temporal sulcus, but notably excluding mPFC.
source: the latter analysis revealed a distinct network including bilateral visual cortex, right superior parietal lobule (SPL), bilateral middle frontal gyrus (MFG), bilateral medial SFG, bilateral parahippocampal cortex (PHC), left fusiform gyrus, right angular gyrus (AG), as well as bilateral posterior superior temporal sulcus, but notably excluding mPFC.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding.

claim: This pattern of results provides converging neural support for the idea that schemas play different roles at encoding and retrieval in supporting memory for story details.
source: This pattern of results provides converging neural support for the idea that schemas play different roles at encoding and retrieval in supporting memory for story details.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the data presented.

claim: Most existing schema research has relied on univariate contrasts of brain activations evoked by schema-consistent vs. schema-inconsistent learning materials.
source: most of this research has relied on univariate contrasts of brain activations evoked by schema-consistent vs. schema-inconsistent learning materials, rather than trying to track the degree to which schematic information is represented for individual stimuli.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior literature.

claim: Existing schema studies have mostly looked at relatively simple forms of schematic knowledge rather than knowledge about the structure of real-world, temporally extended events.
source: Also, existing studies have mostly looked at relatively simple forms of schematic knowledge (e.g., seashells at the beach vs. lamps at a playground; McAndrews et al., 2016) rather than knowledge about the structure of real-world, temporally extended events.
evidence: This is a characterization of prior literature with a citation.

claim: The neural mechanisms of how schemas are instantiated and maintained during unconstrained memory search for naturalistic events have not been thoroughly explored.
source: Lastly, because existing paradigms have mostly tested memory with recognition or short associative recall tasks, the neural mechanisms of how schemas are instantiated and maintained during unconstrained memory search for naturalistic events have not been thoroughly explored
evidence: This is a characterization of a gap in prior literature.

claim: The use of free recall allowed the study to address a gap in the literature regarding unconstrained memory search.
source: our use of free recall allowed us to address this gap in the literature.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the current study addresses a gap.

claim: Baldassano et al., 2018 identified sequences of neural patterns that are unique to particular stories.
source: A key benefit of this paradigm is that it allowed us to identify sequences of neural patterns that are unique to particular stories (e.g., sequences of patterns that are reliably invoked by a particular airport narrative, more so than by other airport narratives)
evidence: This statement describes a finding from prior work using the same paradigm.

claim: Baldassano et al., 2018 identified sequences of patterns that represent the underlying script.
source: and sequences of patterns that represent the underlying script (e.g., sequences of patterns that are shared across different airport narratives, more so than across restaurant and airport narratives).
evidence: This statement describes a finding from prior work using the same paradigm.

claim: Baldassano et al., 2018 identified a range of areas that represented schematic information in a modality-independent fashion.
source: Baldassano et al., 2018 leveraged this to identify a range of areas that represented schematic information (i.e., restaurant vs. airport) in a modality-independent fashion.
evidence: This statement describes a finding from prior work.

claim: Of the regions of interest investigated by Baldassano et al., 2018, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) was the only one that was sensitive to the specific temporal order of events in a schema.
source: Of the regions of interest (ROIs) investigated, medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) was the only one that was sensitive to the specific temporal order of events in a schema.
evidence: This statement describes a finding from prior work.

claim: The current study extends the Baldassano et al., 2018 results by analyzing neural and behavioral data from a separate phase of the experiment in which participants were scanned while freely recalling each of the 16 narratives.
source: Here, we extend the Baldassano et al., 2018 results by analyzing neural and behavioral data from a separate phase of the experiment (not reported in the 2018 study) in which participants were scanned while freely recalling each of the 16 narratives.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the current study extends prior work.

claim: The current study looked at how schemas are represented in the brain during recall.
source: This allowed us to look at how schemas are represented in the brain during recall, and how neural measures of schema representation at encoding and recall are related to recall of specific story details, on a story-by-story basis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the goals of the current study.

claim: The current study examined how neural measures of schema representation at encoding and recall are related to recall of specific story details, on a story-by-story basis.
source: This allowed us to look at how schemas are represented in the brain during recall, and how neural measures of schema representation at encoding and recall are related to recall of specific story details, on a story-by-story basis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the goals of the current study.

claim: Previous studies have shown that greater levels of mPFC activation at encoding are associated with better memory for schema-consistent stimuli.
source: Previous studies have shown that greater levels of mPFC activation at encoding are associated with better memory for schema-consistent stimuli (e.g., Raykov et al., 2021; van Kesteren et al., 2013; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Brod and Shing, 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The current results extend the literature by revealing a within-subjects (across-story) relationship between the activation of anterior mPFC schema representations at encoding and memory for details of temporally extended naturalistic stimuli.
source: our results extend the literature by revealing a within-subjects (across-story) relationship between the activation of anterior mPFC schema representations at encoding and memory for details of temporally extended naturalistic stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the current findings extend prior work.

claim: The findings are compatible with the idea that mPFC might provide a schematic scaffold to which detailed representations are attached at encoding.
source: These findings are compatible with the idea that mPFC might provide a schematic scaffold to which detailed representations are attached at encoding (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Schlichting and Preston, 2015; van Kesteren et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theoretical work.

claim: Increased attention to visual features may reflect stronger schema representation, leading to improved memory encoding.
source: It is possible that certain visual features (e.g., visual features of security lines for airports, or tables for restaurants) are central to the mental representations of these airport and restaurant schemas; as such, increased attention to these visual features (for movies) and/or visualization of these features (for audio narratives) may reflect stronger schema representation, leading to improved memory encoding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the visual cortex findings.

claim: Posterior hippocampus plays an especially important role in representing story-specific details.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that posterior hippocampus plays an especially important role in representing story-specific details, consistent with theories of gist vs. detail representations in the hippocampus (Guo and Yang, 2020; Audrain and McAndrews, 2020; Poppenk et al., 2013; Brunec et al., 2018; Schlichting et al., 2015; Collin et al., 2015; Sekeres et al., 2018; for data suggesting a reversed gradient, see Tompary and Davachi, 2017; Dandolo and Schwabe, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theoretical work.

claim: Left fusiform gyrus and AG have been associated with visual imagery.
source: Left fusiform gyrus and AG have been associated with visual imagery (Spagna et al., 2021; Ragni et al., 2020; Kuhl and Chun, 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Posterior parietal regions such as SPL have been implicated in top-down attention during episodic memory retrieval.
source: and posterior parietal regions such as SPL have been implicated in top-down attention during episodic memory retrieval (Hutchinson et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2005; Cabeza et al., 2008) and general memory success (Brod et al., 2015; Webb et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Participants may need to rely on top-down generation of visual cues to orient to particular schema stages during recall.
source: Because no visual cue (apart from the title of a story) was provided during recall, participants may need to rely on top-down generation of visual cues to orient to particular schema stages (e.g., generating a mental image of what airport security usually looks like, to cue memory for the airport security part of an airport narrative).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the retrieval findings.

claim: Some studies have found that schema-related activity in mPFC during retrieval benefits memory.
source: While some studies have found that schema-related activity in mPFC during retrieval benefits memory (Brod et al., 2015; van Kesteren et al., 2010b; Müller et al., 2020; Webb et al., 2019; Raykov et al., 2021), others have not (van Buuren et al., 2014; Webb et al., 2016; Guo and Yang, 2020; van der Linden et al., 2017; Reagh et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement characterizes mixed findings in prior literature with citations.

claim: The current study did not observe strong mPFC schema reinstatement during retrieval.
source: In our study, we did not observe strong mPFC schema reinstatement, nor were we able to relate it to a behavioral memory benefit.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a null finding.

claim: The current study was not able to relate mPFC schema reinstatement to a behavioral memory benefit.
source: In our study, we did not observe strong mPFC schema reinstatement, nor were we able to relate it to a behavioral memory benefit.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a null finding.

claim: It is possible that schema representations in mPFC contribute to retrieval, but the study failed to detect this contribution.
source: It is possible that schema representations in mPFC contribute to retrieval, but we failed to detect this contribution, for example, because they only emerge at specific time points during recall, or they only arise after sleep consolidation (van der Linden et al., 2017; Brod et al., 2015; van Kesteren et al., 2010b), or they contribute through interactions with other brain regions (Guo and Yang, 2020; van Kesteren et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the null finding with citations to prior work.

claim: Schematic representations in mPFC during recall may be associated less with accurate recall of specific story details and more with verbal descriptions of schematic elements of the narrative.
source: Alternatively, schematic representations in mPFC during recall may be associated less with accurate recall of specific story details and more with verbal descriptions of schematic elements of the narrative.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the null finding.

claim: The rubric used for scoring memory performance tracks recall of story-specific details.
source: Because the rubric we made for scoring memory performance tracks recall of story-specific details, it is not ideal for measuring the extent to which a recall conforms to the general (restaurant or airport) schema.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the behavioral measure used.

claim: The rubric is not ideal for measuring the extent to which a recall conforms to the general schema.
source: Because the rubric we made for scoring memory performance tracks recall of story-specific details, it is not ideal for measuring the extent to which a recall conforms to the general (restaurant or airport) schema.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a limitation of the behavioral measure.

claim: Baldassano et al., 2018 found that schema representation at encoding across many of the same regions was modality-independent.
source: Baldassano et al., 2018 found that schema representation at encoding across many of the same regions reported here (Figure 2) was modality-independent.
evidence: This statement describes a finding from prior work.

claim: The across-modality analysis reproduced results previously reported by Baldassano et al., 2018.
source: We therefore introduced a variant of our main analysis in which we contrasted schematic representations across-modality (i.e., video story vs. audio stories; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and found that this contrast reproduced results previously reported (Baldassano et al., 2018) and corroborated the results reported in the main text.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a supplementary analysis.

claim: The across-modality analysis corroborated the results reported in the main text.
source: We therefore introduced a variant of our main analysis in which we contrasted schematic representations across-modality (i.e., video story vs. audio stories; Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and found that this contrast reproduced results previously reported (Baldassano et al., 2018) and corroborated the results reported in the main text.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a supplementary analysis.

claim: When relating across-modality neural schema scores to behavior, positive relationships to memory performance in mPFC at encoding were found.
source: When we related these across-modality neural schema scores to behavior (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), we again found positive relationships to memory performance in mPFC at encoding
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a supplementary analysis.

claim: Among a sparser set of regions at recall, a positive relationship to memory in anterior hippocampus was found in the across-modality analysis.
source: among a sparser set of regions at recall, we also found a positive relationship to memory in anterior hippocampus, suggesting that hippocampus can generalize across both content (i.e., shared structure across stories) and the surface form of content (i.e., modality).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a supplementary analysis with an interpretation.

claim: Hippocampus can generalize across both content (i.e., shared structure across stories) and the surface form of content (i.e., modality).
source: among a sparser set of regions at recall, we also found a positive relationship to memory in anterior hippocampus, suggesting that hippocampus can generalize across both content (i.e., shared structure across stories) and the surface form of content (i.e., modality).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the across-modality findings.

claim: Prior work has shown that between-subject analyses can improve signal-to-noise ratios while revealing shared representations across people.
source: Prior work has also shown that between-subject analyses can improve signal-to-noise ratios while revealing shared representations across people (Baldassano et al., 2018; Baldassano et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017; Simony et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The results of the within-subject analyses were generally consistent with the between-subject results reported in the main text.
source: the results of these within-subject analyses were generally consistent with the between-subject results reported in the main text, with a few exceptions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a supplementary analysis.

claim: In contrast to the between-subject results, there was no significant relationship between mPFC encoding schema scores and behavior in the within-subject analysis.
source: First, in contrast to the between-subject results, there was no significant relationship between mPFC encoding schema scores and behavior.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a difference between within-subject and between-subject analyses.

claim: The negative relationship between encoding schema scores in posterior hippocampus and subsequent memory was no longer significant in the within-subject analysis.
source: Also, the negative relationship between encoding schema scores in posterior hippocampus and subsequent memory was no longer significant (but the positive relationship between reinstatement schema scores in posterior hippocampus and subsequent memory was still significant).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a difference between within-subject and between-subject analyses.

claim: The positive relationship between reinstatement schema scores in posterior hippocampus and subsequent memory was still significant in the within-subject analysis.
source: Also, the negative relationship between encoding schema scores in posterior hippocampus and subsequent memory was no longer significant (but the positive relationship between reinstatement schema scores in posterior hippocampus and subsequent memory was still significant).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a result that was consistent between within-subject and between-subject analyses.

claim: The current study derived neural measures of story-specific and schematic representations in the brain during the perception and recall of narratives conforming to naturalistic event schemas.
source: In our study, we derived neural measures of story-specific and schematic representations in the brain during the perception and recall of narratives conforming to naturalistic event schemas.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing the study's approach.

claim: The results extend the literature on the benefits of schemas for memory performance.
source: Our results extend the literature on the benefits of schemas for memory performance, relating the maintenance of schematic representations to a continuous behavioral measure of detailed memory for realistic narrative stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: The study related the maintenance of schematic representations to a continuous behavioral measure of detailed memory for realistic narrative stimuli.
source: Our results extend the literature on the benefits of schemas for memory performance, relating the maintenance of schematic representations to a continuous behavioral measure of detailed memory for realistic narrative stimuli.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study's approach.

claim: The study found converging support for the idea that schema representations in mPFC play an important role in memory encoding.
source: We found converging support for the idea that schema representations in mPFC play an important role in memory encoding
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing a key finding.

claim: The study found striking differences between regions where schema representation at encoding was useful for memory, and regions where schema representation at retrieval was useful for memory.
source: but also striking differences between regions where schema representation at encoding was useful for memory, and regions where schema representation at retrieval was useful for memory.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing a key finding.

claim: These findings can serve as a foundation for future work that seeks to further delineate the contributions of these encoding-specific and retrieval-specific schema networks.
source: These findings can serve as a foundation for future work that seeks to further delineate the contributions of these encoding-specific and retrieval-specific schema networks.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Both at encoding and at recall, the ability to predict recall behavior based on neural schema scores and neural story scores (together) was better than prediction based on neural story scores alone.
source: Importantly, follow-up analyses revealed that, both at encoding and at recall, our ability to predict recall behavior based on neural schema scores and neural story scores (together) was better than prediction based on neural story scores alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of a supplementary analysis.

claim: Neural schema representations provide an extra benefit to recall, beyond what is obtained by merely representing story-specific details.
source: This implies that neural schema representations provide an extra benefit to recall, beyond what is obtained by merely representing story-specific details.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the nested model comparison results.

claim: The mechanism by which schemas provide an extra benefit to recall may be different at encoding and recall.
source: The fact that different regions were involved at encoding and recall suggests that the mechanism by which schemas provide this extra benefit may be different at encoding and recall.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the finding that different regions were involved at encoding and recall.

claim: The results of this study do not speak to the validity of theories about how schemas benefit encoding and retrieval.
source: The results of this study do not speak of the validity of either theory – more specialized designs will be needed to test these accounts.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: The schema literature in fMRI has been mostly split between studies that investigate the role of schemas at encoding and those that investigate their role in retrieval.
source: The schema literature in fMRI has been mostly split between studies that investigate the role of schemas at encoding and those that investigate their role in retrieval (but see Bonasia et al., 2018; Sommer, 2017; van der Linden et al., 2017; Raykov et al., 2021; Reagh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior literature with citations.

claim: In contrast to past work, the current design employed naturalistic, temporally extended schema-consistent stimuli that were then paired with realistic unpaced verbal recall.
source: In contrast to this past work, our design employed naturalistic, temporally extended schema-consistent stimuli that were then paired with realistic unpaced verbal recall.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how the current study differs from prior work.

claim: The current design allowed the study to neurally estimate the degree of story-specific and schematic representation for each individual story, at both encoding and retrieval, across cortex and also in hippocampus.
source: Importantly, our design allowed us to neurally estimate the degree of story-specific and schematic representation for each individual story, at both encoding and retrieval, across cortex and also in hippocampus
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the current study design.

claim: The study was able to explore how story-specific and schematic representations related to behavioral memory for story details in a story-by-story fashion.
source: we were able to leverage this to explore how all of these factors related to behavioral memory for story details in a story-by-story fashion.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the capabilities of the current study design.

claim: Schema representations were present at encoding in mPFC.
source: As was shown in a previous analysis of this dataset (Baldassano et al., 2018), schema representations were present at encoding in many regions previously identified in other studies of schemas, including mPFC (van Kesteren et al., 2013; van Kesteren et al., 2020; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Raykov et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017; Brod and Shing, 2018; Sommer, 2017; Bonasia et al., 2018; Reagh et al., 2021)
evidence: This statement is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Schema representations were present at encoding in PMC.
source: PMC (Maguire et al., 1999; van Kesteren et al., 2013; Sommer, 2017; Bonasia et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Schema representations were present at encoding in SFG.
source: SFG (Bonasia et al., 2018; Brod and Shing, 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Schema representations were present at encoding in PHC.
source: PHC (Keidel et al., 2018; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Bonasia et al., 2018; van der Linden et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Schema representations were present at encoding in AG.
source: AG (Keidel et al., 2018; Bonasia et al., 2018; van der Linden et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Schema representations were present at encoding in the hippocampus.
source: and the hippocampus (van Kesteren et al., 2013; van Kesteren et al., 2014; Raykov et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by the current data and citations to prior literature.

claim: The study identified strong schema representation in prostriata.
source: We also identified strong schema representation in prostriata (Mikellidou et al., 2017), a region anterior to V1 and in between restrosplenial cortex (RSC) and PHC.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a finding with a citation describing the region.

claim: Prostriata is a region anterior to V1 and in between restrosplenial cortex (RSC) and PHC.
source: We also identified strong schema representation in prostriata (Mikellidou et al., 2017), a region anterior to V1 and in between restrosplenial cortex (RSC) and PHC.
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the anatomical location of prostriata with a citation.

claim: The study found multiple regions in which maintenance of abstract schematic information was associated with improved memory for story details.
source: However, we found multiple regions in which maintenance of this abstract schematic information was associated with improved memory for story details, including anterior mPFC, lateral frontal cortex, and portions of visual cortex (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding.

claim: Two independent coders scored every participant's memory performance with an intercoder reliability of Pearson r = 0.95.
source: Two independent coders scored every participant's memory performance (intercoder reliability, Pearson r = 0.95), and final scores per story were averaged across both independent coders.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the reliability of the behavioral coding.

claim: Final memory scores per story were averaged across both independent coders.
source: Two independent coders scored every participant's memory performance (intercoder reliability, Pearson r = 0.95), and final scores per story were averaged across both independent coders.
evidence: This is a direct statement about how behavioral scores were computed.

claim: All data is openly available for download at OpenNeuro.
source: All data is openly available for download at OpenNeuro.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.

claim: Scripts used for analysis are available at GitHub.
source: Scripts used for analysis also available at GitHub, (copy archived at swh:1:rev:af3cf26ee9a82ffa898708ecc3c2cfdfd9bd6633; Masís-Obando, 2021).
evidence: This is a direct statement about code availability.
